extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century British periodical readership
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prescriptive observations embedded in The Spectator essays about temperament, conduct, and what is fit to report or remark upon in a public periodical. Useful as a model for composing short, didactic, character-driven essays for a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication criterion for dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: People may dream on as long as they please, but I shall take no Notice of any Imaginary Adventures that do not happen while the Sun is on this Side of the Horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor limits coverage of 'dream' anecdotes to those occurring in daytime (or at least while the sun is up). Example: the author 'stifles Fritilla's Dream at Church' because it did not meet this standard. Anti-pattern: publishing sensational nocturnal fantasies without relevance to waking behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make advantageous use of morning interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead therefore of suppressing this Order of Mortals, I would propose it to my Readers to make the best Advantage of their Morning Salutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noisy morning criers and watchmen should be regarded as remembrancers that admonish people to return from fancied states to their real condition. Use such interruptions to ground characters or narrators in reality rather than silencing them outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate imagination to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing the Imagination through all its Extravagancies, whether in Sleeping or Waking, is no improper Method of correcting and bringing it to act in Subordinancy to Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow imaginative excursions as a means to discipline and refine them so that imagination delights only in objects compatible with cool, sedate judgment. Example: examine dreams and fancies to correct excesses rather than merely censoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and moderation of mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: The merry Part of the World are very amiable, whilst they diffuse a Chearfulness through Conversation at proper Seasons and on proper Occasions; but... a great Grievance to Society, when they infect every Discourse with insipid Mirth, and turn into Ridicule such Subjects as are not suited to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour and levity must be timed and applied to suitable subjects; overuse or misapplied mirth becomes folly. Antipatterns: indiscriminate ridicule, injecting levity into solemn matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness must be humane and timely
rubrics_metrics.description: Seriousness has its Beauty whilst it is attended with Chearfulness and Humanity, and does not come in unseasonably to pall the good Humour of those with whom we converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A serious tone is valuable when it remains compassionate and does not spoil social good humour by being out of place. Avoid solemnity that is brusque, joyless, or poorly timed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes; combine merry and serious
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Man's Temper were at his own Disposal, I think he would not chuse to be of either of these Parties; since the most perfect Character is that which is formed out of both of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal character (and by implication, a well-crafted essay or persona) blends cheerfulness and seriousness—neither hermit-like melancholy nor perpetual buffoonery. Strive for balance in tone and characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levity weakens virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Levity of Tamper takes a Man off his Guard, and opens a Pass to his Soul for any Temptation that assaults it. It favours all the Approaches of Vice, and weakens all the Resistance of Virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against excessive levity as a moral and psychological danger; in character portrayal, show how unchecked frivolity can lead to imprudence or vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and role suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A Comedian ... fancied that he should succeed very well in it, if he could strike two or three laughing Features out of his Face: He tried the Experiment, but contracted so very solid a Look ... that I am afraid he will be fit for no Part hereafter but a Timon of Athens, or a Mute in the Funeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering one's habitual temperament to fit a role may produce awkwardness or unsuitability. In dramatic or character writing, be mindful that forced changes of demeanour can backfire and create implausible portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative anecdote as moral proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous short tales (chimney-sweeper deposing an emperor in a dream; watchman freeing a man from enemies; small-coalman saving a man from imprisonment) are used to demonstrate consequences of waking interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, concise anecdotes—sometimes absurd—to illustrate a moral point or to show practical consequences of abstract claims. Antipattern: relying solely on abstract argument without concrete illustrative instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing benevolence requires persistent practice
rubrics_metrics.description: However, a great deal may be done by a Course of Beneficence obstinately persisted in; this, if any thing, being a likely way of establishing a moral Habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good habits of charity and goodwill must be continually reinforced; intermittent practice allows nature to reclaim its previous tendency. For persuasive writing on moral improvement, emphasise steady practice over one-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of the world undermines benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Another Thing which suspends the Operations of Benevolence, is the Love of the World; proceeding from a false Notion Men have taken up, that an Abundance of the World is an essential Ingredient into the Happiness of Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that worldly wealth breeds distrust and competition; contrast worldly goods (which diminish by division) with virtue (which grows by sharing). Use this contrast as a rhetorical device to promote civic generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm mind required for beneficence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneasiness of any Kind... hath not Leisure to attend to the Necessity or Reasonableness of a Kindness desired, nor a Taste for those Pleasures which wait on Beneficence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray tranquil, contented characters as more disposed to generosity; disturbed or anxious minds are less capable of benevolence. In advice essays, counsel readers toward remedies for uneasiness to restore charitable impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of pleasures as a criterion for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Soul consists of many Faculties... Every Faculty is as a distinct Taste in the Mind, and hath Objects accomodated to its proper Relish... who can question but that there is an infinite Variety in those Pleasures we are speaking of?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing human happiness (or depicting an ideal afterlife), emphasise variety that satisfies diverse faculties—intellect, memory, imagination, devotion, social affection. Use hierarchical and multi-faceted descriptions rather than a single repetitive pleasure.
